NADIA KOVACS
Senior Program Manager, Supply Chain Software
Columbus, Ohio | nadia.kovacs@example.com | 555-0142

SUMMARY
Program manager with nine years in warehouse, returns and fulfilment software. I take messy multi-site rollouts and turn them into programs with a plan, a budget and a weekly rhythm that operations teams actually follow. Strongest at working between engineering, warehouse floor staff and vendors.

EXPERIENCE

Tallgrass Logistics - Senior Program Manager, Returns Platform (Sep 2021 - present)
- Led the migration of 14 regional warehouses onto a single returns-processing platform over 16 months, on a $2.4M program budget, with a cross-functional team of 9 (4 engineers, 3 warehouse leads, 1 analyst, 1 vendor manager).
- Proposed a same-day triage rule for returned items after shadowing night-shift staff for two weeks. Piloted at two sites, then rolled out to all 14. Average returns processing time fell from 6.4 days to 4.4 days (31 percent).
- Renegotiated terms with 3 carriers, saving about $610,000 a year.
- Missed the original go-live for the Midwest cluster by six weeks in 2023 after underestimating vendor API rate limits. Rebuilt the cutover plan, added a load-testing gate that is now required on every program, and shipped the cluster with no customer-facing outage.
- Mentored 3 junior coordinators; two have since been promoted.

Fernhill Software - Program Manager, Warehouse Systems (Jun 2018 - Feb 2021)
- Delivered a handheld scanner rollout across 6 sites and 220 devices, on schedule and 4 percent under a $780,000 budget.
- Built a weekly operations dashboard adopted by 40 site managers; escalations to engineering dropped 22 percent in the first two quarters.
- Ran the customer-facing incident review for warehouse outages, a role I took on because nobody else owned it.

Cobalt Bay Systems - Operations Analyst (Jul 2015 - May 2018)
- Built a forecasting model for inbound freight that improved dock scheduling accuracy by 12 percent.
- Wrote the first standard operating procedures for the Portland cross-dock, later reused at two other sites.

CAREER BREAK (Feb 2021 - Sep 2021)
Relocated from Portland to Columbus and spent time supporting a parent through a health issue. Completed the Supply Chain Analytics Certificate (120 hours, Ridgemont Extension) and built a Python simulation of warehouse slotting that I later used at Tallgrass.

EDUCATION AND CERTIFICATIONS
B.S. Industrial Engineering, Ridgemont State University, 2015
Project Management Professional (PMP), 2019
Supply Chain Analytics Certificate, Ridgemont Extension, 2021

SKILLS
Program planning, vendor negotiation, SQL, Python (analysis and simulation), Jira, dashboard design, stakeholder communication, incident review facilitation.

VOLUNTEER
Central Ohio Food Network, logistics volunteer (2019 - present). Rebuilt the volunteer scheduling process and reduced no-shows by 35 percent.

SUMMARY OF RESIDENTIAL LEASE - UNIT 4C, HARBOR LANE APARTMENTS

Tenant: Jordan Vale. Landlord: Beacon Row Property Management (fictional).
Lease term: 12 months, starting 1 March through the last day of February.
Monthly rent: $1,640, due on the first of each month. A late fee of $60 applies after the fifth day.
Security deposit: $1,640, refundable within 30 days of move-out less documented damage.
Utilities: Tenant pays electricity and internet. Landlord covers water, sewer and trash.
Parking: One assigned space, number 27. Guest parking is limited to 48 hours.
Pets: One cat under 12 pounds allowed with a $300 non-refundable pet fee. No dogs.
Maintenance: Non-emergency requests are answered within three business days through the resident portal. Emergencies (no heat, flooding) are answered within four hours by the on-call line.
Renewal: Tenant must give written notice 60 days before the end of the term if not renewing. Otherwise the lease converts to month-to-month at a rate of $1,715.
Early termination: Permitted with 45 days notice and payment of two months' rent.
Quiet hours: 10 pm to 7 am. No smoking anywhere inside the building.
Move-out: Tenant must schedule a walkthrough at least one week before the end of the term. Cleaning charges of up to $185 apply if the unit is not returned in move-in condition.
Guests: Any guest staying longer than 14 consecutive days must be added to the lease.
Contact: office hours are weekdays 9 am to 5 pm; the portal is monitored on weekends for emergencies only.

FJOB-CTX-G1.title: Portfolio case study: Saltmarsh offline field inspections
FJOB-CTX-G1.text:
PORTFOLIO CASE STUDY - SALTMARSH: OFFLINE-FIRST FIELD INSPECTIONS
My role: mobile and sync engineer (1 of 3 engineers). Timeline: April 2024 - January 2025.

THE PROBLEM
Ferrow County Water Authority sends inspectors out to check backflow valves, hydrants and meter vaults. Before Saltmarsh they filled in paper forms, then retyped them at the office. About a third of the sites have no cell signal at all, so an online-only app was never going to work. There were 42 inspectors when we started.

WHAT WE BUILT
- A React Native app (iOS and Android) that stores every inspection in SQLite on the device and works fully offline.
- A small Go sync service in front of PostgreSQL.
- A web dashboard for supervisors (built by my teammate Ines Carvalho; I only touched the export endpoint).

THE PART I OWNED: THE SYNC ENGINE
- Every record is split into fields, and each field carries its own version stamp: a hybrid logical clock value plus the device ID.
- When two inspectors edit the same inspection offline, the server merges field by field. If they changed different fields, both edits survive. If they changed the same field, the higher clock wins and the losing value is kept in a "conflict shelf" that the supervisor sees on the dashboard.
- Photos never conflict: they are append-only and keyed by a content hash, so a re-upload after a dropped connection is a no-op.
- Sync runs in batches of 50 records with a resumable cursor, so a sync that dies halfway through a canyon picks up where it stopped.
- In the first 6 months after launch, 214 field-level conflicts went to the conflict shelf. Supervisors overrode the automatic winner 9 times.

RESULTS
- Average time per inspection went from 26 minutes to 11 minutes (the county's own time study, 3 weeks before and 3 weeks after).
- Crash-free sessions went from 97.1% in the beta to 99.6% at the 1.0 release.
- Retyping at the office went away entirely; the county reassigned one clerk position to scheduling.

WHAT WENT WRONG
- In version 1.3 I shipped on-device photo compression to cut upload size. It worked, but it ran on the main thread at full resolution and drained batteries: inspectors reported phones dying by early afternoon. I rolled it back within 4 days, then moved compression to a background worker that only runs while charging. My lesson: I tested on a new phone plugged into my desk, not on a three-year-old phone in the field in August.
- I underestimated how long the Android permission flow for background location would take to get through review. We slipped the 1.0 date by two weeks.

WHAT I WOULD DO DIFFERENTLY
- Put a field test with real inspectors into every release, not just the big ones.
- Write the conflict rules down as a one-page spec earlier. We argued about "last writer wins" for weeks before agreeing on per-field clocks.

STACK
React Native, TypeScript, SQLite (op-sqlite), Go, PostgreSQL, Sentry, GitHub Actions, Fastlane.

items.question: Tell me about a time you worked on a team where not everyone pulled their weight.
items.answer: When someone on a team isn't pulling their weight, I start by assuming there's something I don't know yet, so I go to them directly and privately before it becomes a group problem. I ask what's getting in the way and whether the work is clear, because sometimes it's a blocker or a misunderstanding rather than effort. If it's real and it keeps happening, I'd rather be honest with them early than let it quietly build resentment on the team, and I'd loop in a lead if it needs to go further. What I care about is the team staying functional and the person getting a fair shot before anything escalates.

items.role: USER: the job candidate. OTHER PARTY: the interviewer / recruiter. Natively: what the candidate says, in first person. Résumé/JD (if in evidence) are the candidate's own.
items.question: Which of my past jobs is the best example for this role?
items.answer: I can't point to a specific past job without your résumé or the job description in front of me, so let me answer it the way I'd actually think about it. The best example is whichever role lines up most closely with what this job needs day to day, not the most impressive title. I'd look at the core responsibilities here, then pick the role where I did the most of that same work, and lead with it. If you add your résumé and the target job description under Profile Intelligence in Settings, I can name the exact role.

items.question: Who should own this?
items.answer: Ownership should sit with whoever is closest to the outcome and can actually make the call, not whoever has the most context by default. I'd want one clear owner with the authority to decide, and everyone else contributing input rather than sharing the decision. If it's genuinely cross-team, I'd name a single accountable person and let them pull in the others.

items.question: What's the achievement on your resume you're proudest of? Walk me through it.
items.answer:
The one I'm proudest of is the same-day triage rule at Tallgrass. I spent two weeks shadowing the night-shift staff, and it was clear the real delay was how returned items got sorted, not the volume. I proposed a same-day triage rule, piloted it at two sites, then rolled it out to all 14. Average returns processing time went from 6.4 days to 4.4 days, about 31 percent.

What made it stick was starting small and letting the pilot prove it before asking anyone to change how they worked.

items.question: Just once?
conversation: INTERVIEWER: I've got a hard stop at three today, just so you know.
USER (spoken): No problem.
INTERVIEWER: Great, let's get into it.
INTERVIEWER (heard): Tell me about a time you worked under intense pressure.

NATIVELY: I don't have a specific story from my background that fits this well, so let me tell you how I actually operate under pressure. I get very deliberate about triage: I figure out what genuinely has to happen first and what can wait, I communicate early with whoever's affected so nobody's surprised, and I keep the scope tight rather than trying to do everything at once. The thing I've learned is that pressure usually gets worse when people go quiet, so I'd rather over-communicate than disappear into the work.
INTERVIEWER (heard): How did you stay calm?

NATIVELY: I stay calm by narrowing my focus. Instead of holding the whole problem in my head at once, I pick the one thing that has to happen next and do that, then the next. And I keep talking to people, because staying in contact with whoever's affected keeps me grounded rather than spiraling on my own.
items.answer: No, it's a pattern, not a one-off. I don't have a single story I'd point to, but the way I handle pressure is consistent: narrow to the next thing, keep people in the loop, and don't go quiet. That's held up across everything I've worked on.

items.question: What should I say about working with difficult teammates?
items.answer: When I'm working with someone difficult, I try to separate the person from the problem. I get curious about what's actually driving the friction, then deal with it directly and privately, one specific issue at a time. I stay calm, keep my side of the work solid, and focus on what we both need to get done.

I'd pull the team together, re-check what's now the priority, and reset the plan around that instead of pushing the old one. I'd rather flag the tradeoffs early, what we're dropping or delaying, than quietly absorb the change and miss the new target.

From there I break the work into the smallest pieces I can validate early, so I'm not guessing for long stretches. I'd rather ask a few sharp questions up front and move than sit still waiting for a brief that may never come.

After that I build the check into how I work, so the same shortcut doesn't happen twice.

items.question: What should I say when they ask about a time I took ownership without being asked?
items.answer: When something's clearly going to fall through the cracks, I don't wait to be asked. I flag it, say what I think needs to happen, and take the first step myself, then loop in whoever needs to know. I'd rather raise it early and be wrong than let it sit. The part I'm careful about is not stepping on someone else's work, so I check whether it's genuinely unowned before I move. That's how I think about ownership: noticing the gap and closing it, not just doing my assigned piece well.
